rv.q: Holiday Inn found me cranky and left me otherwise, and there’s really nothing more to say.
Engaging performances, dynamic dancing and a lively orchestra make it the feel-good show of the fall.

"So sweetly wholesome that you experience a sugar rush while watching it, the show is corny and predictable. But it will surely provide a happy diversion for stressed-out theatergoers during the holiday season...Pinkham and Gayer prove an appealing romantic duo, while Bleu displays his formidable singing and dancing chops in his underwritten role...
It's an amiable family show full of warm-hearted sincerity and resolutely old-fashioned values.
Corbin Bleu has a winning muscularity and grace in various tap and ballroom sequences.
More like a prematurely hung Christmas stocking smelling faintly of mothballs.
For those hoping that the Roundabout Theatre Company had ambitions more challenging than perky audience bait to compete with the other moneymaking holiday offerings, well, hope elsewhere.
But all the charm in the world could not compensate for the reverse alchemy that has turned Berlin gold into brass plate, and Holiday Inn into Labor Day.
The songs are a zippy treat, but the clunky dialogue and air of old-time predictability may leave audiences with reservations
It’s slick, synthetic and soulless, a musical full of robotic jokes and devoid of genuine romance.
HOLIDAY INN is unabashed fluff, delectably served up sharp and snazzy from start to finish.

For sentimentalists, traditionalists, and those who seek a musical with symmetry, this is one that glitters and might even prompt theatergoers to whistle, hum, or even sing something familiar, like "Blue Skies..." as they stroll down the staircase and out into the afternoon or evening air.

When Jones' eye-popping steps (at one point, the ensemble even plays jump rope with Christmas garlands) are combined with the sounds of the elegant 13-piece band led by Andy Einhorn, Holiday Inn shimmers with that breathless pleasure only musicals can deliver.
That means the farm becomes a hostelry that's only open for holidays when it also offers fabulous holiday themed shows.
Until then, a short stay at Holiday Inn provides a welcomed getaway.
Flaws and all, "Holiday Inn" leaves you unreservedly happy -- these days, no small feat.
Book yourself into 'Holiday Inn' just to see the pyrotechnics when tap whiz Corbin Bleu dances around.

The characters — who include song-and-dance journeymen Jim and Ted (Bryce Pinkham and Corbin Bleu, taking on the Crosby and Astaire roles, respectively), fame-hungry bleached blonde Lila (Megan Sikora), and fame-shy mousy brunette Linda (Lora Lee Gayer) — are so stock they’re practically cardboard.
If you're in the mood for show that's light-on-its-feet and wall-to-wall Irving Berlin, check into Broadway's 'Holiday Inn.'

"The show is indeed old-fashioned — but in a very pleasant way. It doesn't poke smug fun at itself, or, at the other end of the attitude spectrum, pretend with a straight face that tastes haven't changed in 75 years. Rather, it takes an appealing middle ground...
To quote one of the show’s other songs, “there’s plenty to be thankful for” in this crowd-pleasing diversion, it just didn’t capture my heart.
But I can't help wishing those involved had wanted to do more with such tantalizing raw components.
When it works (and the shoes sequence delivers like gangbusters) this musical brings down the house.
"Holiday Inn" is pleasant enough, but when I think of its musical peers from the era - namely "White Christmas" - it's more workaday by comparison.
In the new version, all four leads are too goody-goody to be believed.
But it’ll help to check your sense and sensibility in the coatroom.
But the overall effect is dampened, as if everything but that firecracker number was staged with soggy powder.
This one has the manner, but there's an element of personality missing.

But “Holiday Inn” only occasionally springs to life (usually when Bleu takes center stage and reveals his dashing presence and dancing abilities) and too often feels like another generic jukebox musical or holiday attraction.
“Holiday Inn” is the kind of musical that makes you wish there were fewer holidays in the year.

In those ecstatic moments when they're lost in performing and nothing else seems to matter, the musical's message, which Ted borrows from a French poet, becomes clear: “Now and then it's good to pause in our pursuit of happiness to just be happy.”
Holiday Inn is a place where we can get away from all of that kind of talk.
In the hands of worthy performers and with an excellent orchestra conducted by Andy Einhorn, “Holiday Inn” is welcome fun.
In short, it’s a show filled with the old-time virtues of old-time Broadway musical comedy.
This adaptation of the 1942 film is a welcome addition to the Broadway season.
Holiday Inn is old-fashioned fun any time of the year.
It's a good time for this tap-happy burst of optimism to arrive on Broadway.
(Joan Marcus) NEW YORK—The Roundabout Theatre Company production of the 1942 film with Bing Crosby and Fred Astaire, “Holiday Inn,” will be an early Christmas present for Irving Berlin lovers.

This is a musical you go in humming, That’s because the star is the late composer Irving Berlin. Consider this a medley of some of his greatest hits. “Holiday Inn,” playing at Studio 54, is a film-to-stage adaptation, much as “White Christmas” was a few seasons back. That one has had some success as an annual traveling vehicle.
This is the one to see with the entire family while you are in for holiday fun in the city this Thanksgiving and Christmas.
The new old-fashioned musical is entirely pleasant. It’s fun and fluffy, and has a creamy, sorbet-colored palette that’s pleasing to the eyes.
Lampanelli’s lines particularly zing—“Weight Watchers, as in ‘Wait, watch her gain it all back’ ”—but there’s also pathos and feeing to make this a full meal, smoothly directed by Jackson Gay.
That said, unfortunately, much of the production is fairly dim.
But the show as a whole is lacking in so many of its elements that it fails to satisfy, even on the light-and-fluffy entertainment scale.
Well, the show at Studio 54 isn’t remotely that hellish, but it does have so many liabilities that the line does come to mind.
That doesn't mean that 'Holiday Inn' is anything less than surefire entertainment.
Holiday Inn is fluff that you enjoy while watching but won’t retain for long after leaving the theater.

cn.t: Critics find this old-fashioned Irving Berlin tuner a pleasant but predictable diversion, praising its spectacular tap choreography and feel-good charm while noting its corny book and lack of originality.

sg.ra: SeatPlan names Center Orchestra rows E-G as the best seats overall, citing 'a winning mix of perfect proximity and elevated view over the heads in front' on a good rake with a low stage. Headout notes the 'outstanding inclination' keeps sightlines clear from middle rows. AVFMS Row D seat 2: 'Perfect view with unlimited legroom.' 16-row section seats ~350 of the 413 total; low stage means front rows don't require neck strain.

SeatPlan explicitly names Left and Right Mezzanine as 'the best value seats at the Laura Pels Theatre,' citing cheap tickets vs. central Orchestra with 'a clear and close view.' Only 3 rows (AA/BB/CC), under 100 seats — feels intimate and close to stage. Headout confirms 'very little restriction from the Mezzanine overhang at the back' of the Orchestra, meaning the Mezzanine itself is close/low. Row BB flagged by Headout as a specific value row.
